newsitem.title: UK: Flurry of speculative selling hits aluminium.
newsitem.headline: Flurry of speculative selling hits aluminium.

text.p: The aluminium price hovered precariously just above a two-year low on Tuesday after fresh speculative selling hit the industrial metals sector.
Copper also remained under pressure, but aluminium managed to recover some early losses on the London Metal Exchange (LME).
Traders said aluminium still looked vulnerable after it fell to $1,455 per tonne in early trading and closed down $15 at $1,462.

Dealers said there was no fresh news to prompt the wave of selling, but a rise in LME stocks of 4,700 tonnes did not help. Stocks have risen steadily to 947,625 tonnes from a low of 523,175 tonnes in October last year.
"Everyone sold out and then a sniff of buying came in which prompted light covering. But the bounce is certainly not that convincing," said one LME floor trader.
Data from the International Primary Aluminium Institute was slightly more positive, showing world producer stocks in July fell 33,000 tonnes to 3.342 million from end-June.

Copper prices fell to $1,910 at one stage, a shade above the key support band pegged at $1,900/05. But values rallied to finish at $1,924, down just $3 from Monday. Traders said a fall in stocks of 2,525 tonnes lent some support.

Elsewhere in commodity markets, few prices changed much although benchmark Chicago wheat futures were firmer, rising above $4.50 per bushel. Traders cited as good export prospects and firmer soybeans on cool weather concerns.
December wheat at the Chicago Board of Trade was just under $4.60 around the mid-session after being as low as $4.37 a bushel on Monday.
London gold extended a slide to a morning fixing at $382.45 an ounce, down more than $2 from Monday afternoon and the lowest since July 9, 1996.
It seemed to find support and recovered slightly later. Bullion has weakened on speculative disappointment after it failed to respond to inflationary implications of strong U.S. jobs data last week.
Crude oil prices stayed firm with benchmark North Sea Brent Blend above $22.75 per barrel, supported by strong demand for heating fuel in the northern hemisphere.
